in_context.text: After rejoicing that Gaius walks in the truth (1:3-4), the elder praises how he treats travelling believers. Verse 5 opens a section (1:5-8) commending Gaius for welcoming brethren, even ones he did not know. The next verses urge him to keep sending such workers on their way in a godly manner.

speaker.text: "The elder," the unnamed writer of this letter. Early Christian tradition identifies him as John the apostle.

audience.text: Gaius, a believer the elder calls "wellbeloved" and counts among his children in the faith.

affected.text: Travelling Christian workers, "the brethren" and "strangers," who went out for Christ's name and relied on churches for lodging and help.

what.text: The elder tells Gaius that all he does for visiting brethren, including strangers, is a faithful act. Those visitors later told the church about his love (charity).

events.text: Late first century, when Christian workers travelled from church to church and depended on believers to house them. Domitian was emperor (AD 81-96).

written.text: Traditional: about AD 85-95, near the time of 1 and 2 John. Scholarly: most also place it in the late first century, though some think "the elder" was a church leader other than the apostle.

where.text: The letter does not say where it was written or sent. Early tradition places John's last years in Ephesus, and Gaius likely lived in a church in the province of Asia.

purpose.text: The elder commends Gaius for his faithful care of travelling believers. Later in the letter he contrasts Diotrephes, who refused to receive the brethren and threw out those who did (1:9-10).

big_picture.text: Receiving those who carry the gospel makes believers "fellowhelpers to the truth." Scripture elsewhere urges doing good to all, especially the household of faith.

for_readers.text: Ordinary acts of welcome and support for fellow believers, even unknown ones, count as faithfulness before God. Jesus taught that one faithful in little things is faithful in much.

why_it_matters.text: The word means trusty or faithful, used of the faithful servant or steward set over his master's household. Gaius's hospitality is described in the same terms of trustworthy service.

As a noun it means a foreigner or stranger, the same word Jesus uses in "I was a stranger" (Matt 25:35). It can also describe a guest or a host bound by ties of hospitality. So Gaius welcomed people he did not already know.

Literally a brother from the same womb, the word is also used of fellow members of a people and, in the New Testament, of fellow believers. Here it means Christian workers who went out for Christ's name.

takeaway.text: Faithfulness shows up in practical love: opening your home and helping fellow believers who serve the gospel, even strangers. Such help makes you a partner in the truth.

resolved.reason: The sources list commending Gaius and confronting Diotrephes as separate aims of the letter. None of them says the elder praises Gaius in order to set him against Diotrephes, so the claim presents an interpretation as the letter's stated purpose.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources
